speechtext:
that Bill C-80, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and do pass.
She said: Mr. Speaker, this Bill is an important part of the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in May 1985. It contains substantial amendments to the Excise Tax Act aimed at improving tax fairness, and it proposes changes in the application and rate of federal sales tax in order to increase revenue and thus reduce the deficit. The Bill is a clear reflection of the Government's resolve to achieve the Budget's goals of economic renewal while maintaining tax fairness.
During consideration of the Bill by the Legislative Committee, a number of concerns were voiced regarding the fairness of some of the proposals, especially with respect to the new dividing line between taxable and exempt products. This is an important matter and I would like to take this opportunity to elaborate.
The Committee received representations from a number of sectors affected by the proposals contained in this Bill. Manufacturers of candy and confectionery products expressed their doubts about the decision to repeal the sales tax exemption on their products. They argued that candy and confectionery products should continue to be exempt from sales tax on the same basis as other food products. They suggested that a broader range of snacks be made taxable at a reduced rate. Manufacturers of soft bars appeared before the Committee to express their opposition to the proposal by the candy and confectionery products manufacturers, and their support for the line drawn by the Government between taxable and exempt food products.
Committee members expressed concern about the proposals aimed at restricting the exemption on health products to prescription drugs, products for diabetics and drugs required for the treatment of illnesses that pose a health risk, appearing
on a list drawn up by the federal Government. Present exemption rules have given rise to numerous disputes between the Government and taxpayers regarding proper application of the tax. An increasing number of tax exemptions have been granted in this sector as well, which means that many products which are only indirectly connected with health protection are eligible for the exemption. The Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada appeared before the Committee to propose a number of changes in the budgetary proposals so as to include several major drugs which for purely technical reasons are not eligible for an exemption. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has already promised to review the list from time to time and, if necessary, to add new drugs to the list of tax exempt products.
Representatives from the construction industry expressed their opposition to the repeal of the special exemption formerly allowed on prefabricated construction materials. The prefab concrete and structural steel sectors suggested that instead of paying tax on the sale price, they should be allowed to pay tax on only 60 per cent of the price. However, this proposal would perpetuate many of the problems in drawing the line between exempt and non-exempt products in this sector and would substantially reduce Government revenues. For these reasons, the Government did not accede to the industry's requests. The proposals contained in this Bill guarantee fair taxation of construction materials, since all construction materials are now taxable on the sale price just like other manufactured products.
The Canadian Bar Association proposed a number of changes in the Bill to clarify certain technical provisions and improve others which, in the opinion of the Association, do not achieve the degree of fairness intended. Many of these proposals were adopted by the Committee and are included in the Bill before the House today.
The Government is very pleased with the efforts of these and other groups who made representations and appeared before the Legislative Committee to express their views, and it is most grateful.
While all the representations did not lead to amendments to the Bill, the process has been most helpful. The Members and the people who made representations concerning the provisions in the Bill can be assured that their views will be considered extensively and taken into account whenever further changes to those acts are contemplated.
The tax measures included in last May's budget are aimed at controlling the deficit and more efficiently managing our

February 10, 1986
Excise Tax Act
public affairs so we may reap and maintain the benefits of the economic growth we are now enjoying. Our policies designed to control the deficit and better manage public affairs are part of a comprehensive package for meeting a wide range of economic and financial needs.
The deficit affects and threatens each and every one of us. The burden of deficit control measures must be shared in the broadest possible way, if we are to obtain the desired results. The purpose of the Bill now before us is to help us attain that goal through a broad and fair distribution of tax increases.
The principle of fairness also prevails throughout the extensive system of assessment, opposition and appeal procedures introduced in the legislation. Until now, the Excise Tax Act had no provisions for the assessment of sales and excise taxes, and taxpayers had only limited access to an independent appeal process in cases of litigations. The Bill implements an assessment and appeals system similar to that in the Income Tax system.
Where a taxpayer is not satisfied with his assessment or the handling of an application for refund, he will have access to a well-established process ranging from informal discussions with Revenue Canada officials to court hearings. The new system also protects taxpayers from the collection of disputed amounts until there has been a court decision.
The Bill should also be viewed in the light of other budget proposals announced by the Minister of Finance. Tax increases are combined with reductions in public expenditures that amounted to nearly 75 per cent of the deficit reduction effort in 1985-86, the other 20 per cent provided by tax increases. The impact of tax increases on the economy is mitigated by tax reductions, the freeze on unemployment insurance premiums, the injection into the economy of RHOSP funds, and the important proposals to stimulate private initiative and productive investments in the economy. This Government has openly asked a wide range of taxpayers to shoulder their fair share. Overall, expenditure reductions and tax changes are an important and a fair way to restore this country's financial position.
All Canadians will benefit from the achievement of our goals.

Mr. Speaker, I had intended to make only brief comments on the Bill before us, but since the Minister has rightly pointed out that the Bill must be viewed in a broader context, and since the Minister made her remarks in a fairly broad context, I trust that I will be allowed to do so for just a few minutes.
The Government claims that it wants to reduce the deficit, but what is happening in the Budget as a whole? The Budget does away with tax on the oil multinationals so that by 1990 the Government will forgo $8.5 billion. The Budget does away with tax on capital gains. As a result of this measure, by 1990
the Government will forgo nearly $5 billion in favour of the 4 per cent of the population which can benefit from this measure. At the same time, low and middle-income families and individuals are told to tighten their belts because they must do their share in bringing down the deficit.
The Government considers that it can afford $875 million to bail out uninsured bank depositors. It considers that it can afford tax rulings which may result in billions in of forgone revenue. However, when it comes to families with incomes of $15,000 or $20,000 the Government cannot afford to keep indexing family allowances. The Government thinks it can activate the economy by taking money away from those who have less, the low and middle-income Canadians, and giving it to the wealthy.
I will now turn directly to the provisions of Bill C-80. The avalanche of taxes in this Bill will have a severe dampening effect on the economy. There is no disputing that the broadening of the sales tax base and the tax increases will extract billions of dollars from the domestic economy putting inflationary pressure on the economy and dampening consumer demand. The Government's line has been that it is fair because it hits everyone. The Minister's speech this morning made much of fairness and equity. However, it is plain to see that tax increases and new taxes on items such as health care products hit first and hardest at those on fixed incomes and those earning low and middle incomes. This is not fair. It has been amply demonstrated that this barrage of tax increases cannot be justified economically or on the basis of fairness. It is impossible to understand how a Government that took an unprecedented nine months to bring in its first Budget could have brought in measures so unsound and unfair.
This is not to say that Canadians are not prepared to help get the deficit under control. Of course, all Canadians are concerned about the deficit and about the amount of money that goes out to service the national debt which rose primarily during the time of recession. Of course, since the economy is becoming healthier, this is the logical time to move on the deficit, but not in this way.
What are Canadians to make of a Government that rushes to bail out a bank and the bank's uninsured depositors, and then tells blind people that they must pay sales tax on the food for their seeing-eye dogs in order to get the deficit under control? What deficit reduction will there be when the Government forgoes billions of dollars through tax rulings, bailouts, and so on? The $2 billion to be taxed out of consumers' hands through this measure this year may just about cover the cost of the bank fiasco. What possible justification does the Government have for unmercifully squeezing low and middle-income Canadians on the pretext that they must share in the task of getting our fiscal house in order?
We have addressed the specific measures in this Bill at report stage and there is no need to repeat the arguments which were made then. However, I should point out that all the amendments put forward were voted down solidly by the Government. This morning the Minister sounded a little sympathetic to the case put forward by the confectionary manu-

facturers, although she did not say that they should necessarily be excused from sales tax.
What they have pointed out is that it was difficult for them to have to absorb the tax on the goods they had prepackaged for their peak sales times, Hallowe'en and Christmas. A delay in the imposition of the sales tax would have been greatly appreciated by that industry, but the Government was intransigent.
The Minister seemed to imply this morning that the proposals which concern the construction industry might be looked at in the future. In the meantime, however, we will find many small construction firms in real difficulty. In the construction sector, fixed price contracts are common and those who found themselves suddenly hit with large additional sales taxes have had to absorb them and the amounts are considerable, perhaps enough to put some people out of business. Those industries have also asked for a grandfather clause which would delay the imposition of these sales taxes for those who have contracts without escalator clauses. The Government refused to give even this small relief. I know that some Hon. Members opposite have written to the Minister asking that this hardship on the construction industry be corrected in the next Budget, so we must hope that perhaps the Government may be listening a little harder in the next few months than it has.
With respect to the whole question of the transportation industry, the additional taxes will certainly make it very hard for it to be competitive with U.S. competitors. The taxes on energy conservation and alternative energy are hitting a very vital and relatively new industry which has come into existence in the last 10 years. It employs about 5,000 people, I believe, and has developed interesting new technologies and opportunities to export, but the Government has removed all incentives from that industry as well as created additional hardships, all in the interest of supporting the oil and gas sector. The Minister did mention this morning that the Government has relented somewhat on the sales tax on health products and we may see some further consideration there. But this is too little, too late. The Bill before us proposes additional sales tax on a wide number of commonly used items. It is a measure which hits particularly at families and those of low and middle incomes. It is harsh, unfair and regressive. It is something of which the Government cannot be proud. This is not the way to fight the deficit. We must only hope that in the upcoming Budget some of the worst excesses of this Bill will be corrected.

Mr. Speaker, I am also quite honoured to have an opportunity to say a few words on this last day of debate on Bill C-80, An Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. I would like to preface my remarks by suggesting that the numbers of families which are defined by Statistics Canada as having a family income which places them below the poverty line are actually increasing month by month and have been for some time. The same
Excise Tax Act
statistics tell us that those people who, I suppose, we could call the "super rich" or "extremely wealthy" are also expanding while the group of middle income earners is shrinking by the week and by the month. Fundamentally, this particular Bill which flows out of the last Budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will make the system even more discriminatory against the middle income earner and the poor of Canada.
I think it is instructive to see Bill C-80 in the following light. What we are discussing here today is a Bill which will impose a whole new range of taxes on everyone, rich, middle and low income earners alike. In other words, when we buy a bottle of aspirin or some other similar non-prescription drug, if we purchase some pop for our children or some pet food, if we fill up our gas tank, or buy a new shirt, a refrigerator, or a teapot, we all pay the same level of tax. You and 1 both know, Mr. Speaker, that some people will not even notice the additional few percentage points added to their bill. Others, of course, will. A difference of $2, $3 or $15 makes a real difference to more and more families, especially those families which find themselves living below the poverty line as defined by our own Statistics Canada.
If we examine the provisions of the Bill before us and the other Bills already dealt with in the last few weeks, we find the average Canadian family will now have to pay about $1,000 more in federal taxes, in charges of one kind or another, as a result of this Bill and the two previous Bills. In 1986, the average Canadian family will have nearly $1,000 plucked from their purses, wallets and pocketbooks for the federal Government to use as it sees fit. Allegedly, this is for assistance in reducing the deficit, and I say "allegedly", and I will come back to that point in a few moments.
Some of my colleagues and I have been touring the country on what we call "Tax Probe '86". It is an effort to probe into the tax system and covers sales tax, excise tax of one kind or another, personal tax and corporate tax. We have talked to specialists, tax advisers, lawyers and accountants and those groups which are involved with taxation, whether it be the forest industry, mining industry, construction industry or the trucking industry.
Some very interesting points have emerged. For example, when we suggest to people that their taxes related to the federal Government's activities will result in about a $1,000 increase in their taxes in 1985 and 1986, most people do not know that. I suspect that very few people actually know what is going to happen to them as a result of the taxes. They tell me they find it hard to believe so I break it down for them.
First, we make the assumption of a family of four, with one wage earner bringing home about $35,000. This is an above average family, the middle income earner, the people who once again are being grabbed for more and more taxes. When we eliminate the federal tax reduction that family loses $100 off the top. That, by the way, will be another $100 next year, but for 1986 the elimination of the federal tax reduction will cost a family $100 in money they do not have. The modification to the cost-of-the-living indexing will cost $115. The cut in family

Excise Tax Act
allowance, which is another Bill, will cost $22.50. The broadening of the sales tax will cost about $150. That deserves some comment. Sales tax is the most regressive kind of tax to impose because it hits everyone equally. Those whose income is $1,000 a month and those whose income is $15,000 a month all pay the same sales tax on goods they purchase. That will cost this family an extra $150. Not only has the tax gone up, but it has been broadened to take in a whole number of commodities which hitherto had not been subject to the sales tax imposition.
You might ask what some of the those items are, Mr. Speaker. They include cough syrup, vitamins, aspirins and cold remedies of one kind or another. It is now the middle of winter. How many people here do not know at least somebody who has a cold? Probably half the Members in this House are hacking and sneezing with colds. It is part of the Canadian life, almost, unfortunately. Everybody has to buy cold remedies of one kind or another, but now for the first time these remedies are to be taxed at 11 per cent. Then we have medicated shampoos, surgical gloves, sutures and certain kinds of surgical equipment. This is a federal tax on sick folks, people with bronchial and other problems who need non-prescription drugs. In a country that prides itself in having one of the finest medicare systems in the world, to be taxing people now at 11 per cent for cold remedies and the like seems to be a very regressive step.
What about the increase in gasoline tax? This will amount to an additional $50 in tax in 1986 for a family. A lot has been said about the increase in gasoline tax, but I noticed with some interest that the Canadian Trucking Association said that it will create inflation increases in certian parts of Canada and that it was really a subtle tax on distance. People who live in the more remote areas of the west, the east and the north will feel the gasoline tax more than others. This tax is very discriminatory. The increase in oil and gas prices will amount to about $200.
An increase in the sales tax generally will result in $150 more per household, an increase in unemployment insurance premiums will amount to $102 per household and an increase in cigarette and alcohol tax, assuming people have a few glasses of wine or perhaps the odd sip of this or that during the year, will amount to about $75, making a total tax increase of $964.50, to say nothing of a whole host of other costs. For example, increased user fees in our federal parks and increased ferry charges. One can go on and on with all kinds of newly imposed costs.
On the one hand the Government says, we have real concerns about the deficit and so we are going to introduce a set of new taxes and increase a set of other taxes that are the most regressive. These taxes will have a significant impact on people who can least afford to pay, namely, the poor, those on fixed incomes like the elderly, people of limited means, all those unemployed and those who have part-time work. The people really struggling to make a go of it today are the ones who will be most adversely affected by these impositions. But not
everybody will receive the same imposition, Mr. Speaker. Let us be very clear about that.
At the same time the Minister of Finance was introducing these additional taxes on middle and low-income Canadians, he was also introducing a major income tax break. He is going to remove all the taxes completely for those people able to obtain some or all of their income from capital gains. A person receiving income from capitl gains will be able to receive income of up to half a million dollars and pay no tax whatsoever. Do you not find that to be rather peculiar? On the one hand for deficit reasons-that is the excuse-we have to impose taxes on dog food and on candy bars, taxes that will affect families. Yet on the other hand we are going to give a tax exemption to people who obtain their income from capital gains, up to the accumulated value of income of half a million dollars.

I am glad my friend reminded me of the retirement option for farmers. The Government feels there is another group that needs some assistance in retirement, people whose incomes are about $90,000 a year. The Government has said these folks need help; if you are making only $90,000 a year, we have to give you some incentive to save for your retirement.
The Government in this instance is lifting the limits on the registered retirement savings plans. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, as a wise man, if a person is making $85,000 or $90,000 a year does that person need a tax incentive to encourage him or her to save for retirement? I suspect with an income of that level you could probably take care of yourself using the normal channels and opportunities available. This measure will cost the Government money, make no mistake about it. When you give tax breaks to people who have incomes up to $90,000 a year to encourage them to save for their retirement, it will cost tens, perhaps hundreds of millions of dollars in lost revenue.

If the Government is concerned about the deficit and wants to impose special new taxes on aspirins and cough medicines and hit certain aspects of the construction industry for the first time in some years, I do not see why we should be making exemptions and special deals for some other people.
Let us look at the construction industry. Good grief, 1 remember time and time again one of the points made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was on the campaign trail. Fie said that one of the critical industries of any country is its construction industry. It is an industry that builds, creates new structures, homes, apartments, shops and offices. By building and creating that new landscape, the industry hires a let of people. It is labour intensive and requires all sorts of outlets for manufacturing products for use in those new facilities such as chairs, windows, furnishings and construction material of one kind or another. To encourage the construction industry is a great way not only to create construction jobs, but to create all kinds of other jobs because of the spin-off effect in a variety of other areas.
I remember the Prime Minister saying that one of the ways is to reduce the sales tax on construction material, such a critical area in a country that is trying to expand its economic base. I remember him saying that reducing the sales tax on construction material would be one small thing the federal Government could do. I thought that was a good idea, and I think many people across the country thought that the idea of the Prime Minister to be was a good one. I suspect that most people in the construction industry went out and voted Conservative because they thought it was a good idea to reduce the sales tax on construction material. That industry and those people who listened to those comments were betrayed, because the minute the Minister of Finance had the opportunity to do so, did he reduce the sales tax on construction material? No, he did not. Of all things, he increased it. He said, let us now make it tougher to build in this country; let us impose a new charge on the construction industry so that everyone who builds houses, factories, plants and buildings will be charged more taxes by the federal Government". How on earth will that help anyone? What kind of a signal does that send to the construction industry?
We have committees so that Bills, such as Bill C-80, can be referred to them where we can bring in the advisors and experts to say what will happen as a result of the provisions of the Bill in the construction industry, the soft drink industry, and the dog food and cat food industry. We did that. We said we would co-operate as opposition Members and get the Bill into the committee system as quickly as possible, to hear from those folk who are most knowledgeable about the effects of those provisions. We heard some very interesting things.
We heard from the construction industry that it would cause irreparable damage and set the industry back. As a matter of fact, the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction claimed that it would lose 300 jobs right off the top. The Canadian Prestressed Concrete Institute estimated that 160 jobs would be

lost right off the top because there would be much less activity in building projects. The pet manufacturers indicated that there would be a loss of some 400 jobs, and confectionary manufacturers indicated that up to 1,000 jobs would be lost immediately. Group after group appeared before the committee and said, let us understand one thing; we will lose jobs.
Let me refer to the pet food industry in particular. Thousands of blind Canadians require seeing eye dogs. If the Government is to be totally heartless and impose a new tax on Spot's or Rover's dog food, it should at least exempt seeing eye dogs so that disabled people who require them will not be penalized for having to use and to feed such dogs. Did the people hear that? No, Sir. The Government is to impose a tax on seeing eye dogs. I hear Hon. Members chuckling. I do not believe-

I should like to refer to the alternate energy industry which involves a number of things from windmills to encouraging people to use solar energy and so on. I do not want to put words into the Government's mouth, but I guess it realized the progressive nature of the alternative energy industry. It indicated that there was a need to develop wind, solar, tidal and other alternative forms of energy, but that it would not happen now, and it imposed a new tax on those folk which made it even less competitive and tougher to develop an alternate energy industry. Essentially that is what the Government has done. It imposed an 11 per cent tax in May and an additional 1 per cent in January on the alternate energy business.
I should like to refer to the comments of one person who appeared before the committee. He had the following to say about the decision of the Department of Finance to tax the energy conservation industry:
I do not think they really knew what this industry was all about. When we queried them they were unfamiliar with what photovoltaics was and asked us if we could please describe what microhydro was.
In other words, the Department of Finance was levying taxes without even knowing what it was levying taxes on. That is not the kind of sophistication we would expect from a Government in 1986. That is why we sent it to committee for Fine tuning. Did any government Members pay one iota of attention to these points when they were made? Apparently not.
Perhaps this becomes a little repetitive after a while. We point out time and time again how every group which appeared before the special committee looking into this matter

In closing let me simply say that it seems very hypocritical to be passing Bill C-80 which imposes a set of very regressive taxes that will have a major impact on low and middle-income earners, when at the same time the Government is giving tax breaks to those whose incomes are derived from capital gains-and they are a very small percentage of the taxpayers of the country-and other breaks to large corporations and some very wealthy individuals. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention first that the lapel button I am wearing is a reminder that all Canadians are invited to participate in Winterlude activities now taking place in the national capital. In addition, before commenting briefly on Bill C-80, I urge all my House colleagues to go skating on the canal, admire the outstanding work done by 400 volunteers, and enjoy the entertainment offered in the capital where they should feel right at home.
Mr. Speaker, the House is now on third reading of Bill C-80, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill is yet another indication to Canadians that there is no co-operation between the private sector and the Government, and that the necessary information is lacking. As well it demonstrates quite clearly that recommendations from the industry and Members of the Opposition cut no ice with this Government: the Bill has been before the House for some time now, yet it was reported practically unchanged since it was first introduced on October 18, 1985.
Mr. Speaker, the Government spent the last election campaign wooing Canadian electors and promising them everything under the sun. It kept repeating that the Government would listen to them and promised an open and responsible administration. Promises galore, Mr. Speaker.
Bill C-80 is a rather timely reminder that those promises have not been honoured. The Government did not listen to what the industry had to say. It did not listen to what Hon. Members have been repeating on second reading, in committee, and even today on third reading. No, the Government did not listen, and as a result we have an altogether regressive measure which will put an additional tax burden on the backs of certain Canadians.
It has been said before, Mr. Speaker, and the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) just raised the point that the Government has been anxious to look after the oil multinationals, for example, by lowering taxes to the tune of $8.5 billion. [English]
It is interesting to note that the Budget does away with capital gains of up to $500,000 per Canadian. At the same
time, lower-income families and individuals are told to tighten their belts because they must do their share to bring down the deficit. On top of that, we had the Olympia and York advance ruling which gave it substantial sums of money. Let us total all these give-aways to bank depositors who were uninsured, to multinationals, to Olympia and York and to many others. I think I said at second reading that there is a list that goes on and on and on. That sum of money-$16 billion was given away by this Government to these banks, the oil companies, Olympia and York-adds up to exactly what they are taxing Canadians with in Bill C-80 until 1990.
In other words, if you took the paper that was made public after the last Budget, and you totalled the amount of money given to the oil companies, to the multinationals, given to the banks' depositors, which were uninsured, plus several others 1 have named, you would come up with about the same amount of money.
That is very strange action from a Government which said it would listen, be responsive, and act to protect the interests of all Canadians.

Apparently, Mr. Speaker, we have not yet seen the last of the Conservative Government's regressive measures. There will be higher excise taxes on gas, more taxes on alcoholic beverages, tobacco products, wines, telecommunication programming services, an additional sales tax on a number of building and prefabricated materials, taxes on equipment and building materials used for energy conservation, taxes on candies and soft drinks. Yet such taxes will not apply to certain products widely described as snack foods, so I would predict that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) introduces his Budget in a few days he will be telling us he has found a new formula, a new solution and that, as Ontario has done, he will slap a tax on everything called fast food. There might even be a rationale for that, but he will tax some but no others such as chips and pretzels. I have the complete list here pretzels, potato chips- [English]
What about pretzels, granola bars, nuts and many other things? It is felt not by me, Mr. Speaker, but by the industry itself that they are being discriminated against. Now the Government, and we hear from its branches-I guess they have leaked it-is going to think about putting an over-all tax on all snack food. We will wait and see. I have the Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) say, "No way, no way". We will see. You will have your chance to get up after my speech and ask me a question. I am telling you now that 1 am predicting that this Government will tax pretzels, granola bars and nuts, and will tax all these other things because it creates an enlarged source of income and an enlarged source of taxes.

Mr. Speaker, what 1 find offensive about this Bill-as we know from second reading and also from the report stage-is that, in addition to those things that have been raised by colleagues on this side of the House, it does do two things to the environment that are profoundly disappointing and objectionable. The first one is that the taxes recommended in this Bill will discourage energy conservation, a new and important economic component, and particularly as that affects renewable resources.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that in the seventies, as a result of the oil prices rising in a very short period of time, as a nation we decided to turn to renewable sources of energy and to energy conservation as an important way of reducing our dependence on imported oil, as well as reducing our dependence on non-renewable resources, such as oil and gas. You will recall that in that decade the then Government of Canada launched a variety of initiatives to encourage the formation and the expansion of solar, wind and biomass oriented industries with substantial investments by way of programs aimed at the entrepreneurs who would want to take advantage of it, 1 believe between 1977 and onward. As a result, thre are now in Canada some 450 companies that did not exist 10 years ago actively engaged in the manufacturing, sale and export of equipment related to the use of solar and wind energy and related to the use of solar and wind energy and related renewable sources of energy. That activity, which was made possible because of the creative spirit of many Canadians, has also created some 5,000 jobs.
As if this had not happened, Bill C-80 contains a measure which imposes a new tax on parts and components of the renewable energy industry. It is an imposition that will slow down the expansion of that sector and will affect therefore the creation of jobs. It sends out the wrong signals, because the measure has been interpreted by the members of the association of the solar energy society as being a lack of interest on the part of the Government in renewable sources of energy.
I find it hard to believe that a Government would want to shift to non-renewable resources, as Bill C-80 is implying this Government wants to do. After what was done in the 1970s regarding conservation and renewable energy, it is wrong to give out this message in the mid-1980s when everyone who is engaged in the oil industry is telling us that perhaps four or five years from now prices will rise again. This measure is not only offensive, it does not make sense in terms of the long-term energy interests of our nation.
That is one of my reasons for rising to express my views on Bill C-80. Contained in this Bill is a tax measure that will discourage energy conservation. However, that is only one of the environmental implications of this Bill that must be put on the table for discussion today. The other one is one about which I spoke at the time of second reading of this Bill.
It became evident to me at second reading that we were being asked to endorse and support a tax measure that would

February 10, 1986
Excise Tax Act
impose lower taxes on leaded gasoline and higher taxes on unleaded gasoline. When one purchases unleaded gasoline, one is purchasing a gasoline that is cleaner and more desirable in an environmental sense, because it does not contain a high content of lead and it does not emit substances that find their way into the atmosphere and return to the surface in the form of acid rain. However, when purchasing gasoline we see that there is a difference in price between leaded and unleaded gasoline of some three cents. The unleaded is more expensive. The tax measure introduced by Bill C-80 will make this price gap between the two gasolines even larger.
This increased difference in price will encourage consumers to do two things. First, consumers will be encouraged to engage more frequently in misfuelling, something which the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) quite rightly has criticized, and about which he has expressed himself on more than one occasion by encouraging provinces to introduce legislation that would make it more difficult to misfuel. However, there has been a lack of communication in the Government. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is disregarding the publicly stated objective of the Minister of the Environment by introducing a tax that disregards entirely what the Minister of the Environment has said. The Minister of the Environment has said that we should have gasoline prices at the pump that will not encourage misfuelling and the Minister of Finance has come forward with a proposal that will have the opposite effect.
The second consequence of the gasoline tax measure introduced by Bill C-80 is that people who purchase cars will be looking for cars that consume leaded gasoline rather than unleaded gasoline. Therefore, the sale of leaded gasoline consuming cars will increase and that will result in increased emissions into the environment of lead, something which we all know is a substance that damages the health of humans, and particularly of children. It has been found by a number of scientific studies that lead has a negative and long-term effect on the learning and thinking capabilities of children. As a result of that aspect of it, this measure will also have health implications in the long term, and the Government does not seem to be concerned about that at all.
There are two voices emerging from this so-called Progressive Conservative Government which, regarding environmental matters, is neither progressive nor conservative. The voice of the Minister of the Environment indicates that there should not be any misfuelling and that we should shift our consumption to gasoline that does not contain lead. The other voice which is evidenced by Bill C-80 is proposing the opposite of what any environmentalist or person concerned with health would propose in this day and age.
You may ask, Mr. Speaker, how we may change this and whether or not it has been changed elsewhere. Yes, it can be done and there are nations that have already introduced, by way of changes in their gasoline taxation systems, unleaded gasoline prices which are the same as leaded gasoline prices, and there are nations that are in the process of devising this new system. Once again and for the third time, I must bring
this fact to the attention of the Government and call on the Government to get going in this respect by readjusting the tax structure so as to enable Canadians to find leaded and unleaded gasoline at the same price. The revenue of the state will not be affected or reduced in this way. What will happen is that there will be a shift in the weight of existing taxes, a relief in the taxes imposed on unleaded gasoline and an increase in the taxes imposed on leaded gasoline. Of course, it is possible for someone to detect a flaw and say you can't do that because evidently and inevitably the farmers and the fishermen will be affected. This is a case which we have to recognize in practical terms. In that case we will have to devise a program whereby farmers and fishermen will be refunded the amount they pay additionally on leaded gasoline as a result of these changes in the tax structure presently being imposed on the two types of gasoline. This is the way in which a modern nation has to work.
We have all made speeches on the subject of health and the environment. We have all acknowledged and accepted the reality that lead in gasoline is an element which has long-term negative effects on the health of human beings. We have made commitments to the environment in 1,000 different ways; but when the opportunity arises the political will is missing. Bill C-80 is an example of this. When will the Government show the political will which is needed to practice what it preaches?
We all know that Bill C-80 will move to the Senate after we have dealt with it here. If the Government really wishes to practice what it preaches, then it can make the necessary changes as the Bill progresses through the Senate. We raised the matter in the House in November at second reading stage. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, because you patiently listened to me on the subject, we also raised the issue last week. Your Honour now has to undergo that torture once again. I apologize to you for the frequency and the repetition of the same theme, but I cannot help it. That is the nature of the Bill before us.
If Hon. Members sense me getting a bit hot under the collar and a bit impatient, then they are right. I cannot understand why this point is not taken into account by the Government when it comes to the taxation system. It could correct a situation which is undesirable, namely, the fact that the spread between the price of leaded and unleaded gasoline at the pump is increasing. The spread was 2.5 cents some seven or eight months ago; it is now three cents. Once Bill C-80 is enacted the spread will increase. Therefore, consumers will be given an additional incentive to either misfuel their cars or purchase cars which use leaded gasoline. If this should happen then we will lose the ground which we gained so gradually during the 1970s and the early 1980s. Thus, Hon. Members will not be surprised if one gets up to express these concerns with respect to Bill C-80 from an environmental point of view. I think 1 have done it succinctly enough, both with respect to the tax which is being proposed on renewable energy equipment and with respect to the proposed tax on gasoline. I hope that someone is listening and that remedial action will be taken.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-80 is premised on the belief by this Government that the deficit is the biggest evil. That reminds me of an American comedian who, as part of his act, dresses up as a woman and calls himself Geraldine. Although she is a believer, she always blames the devil: "The devil made me do it". This Government has coined a new phrase: The deficit made me do it. The deficit made me increase taxes. The deficit made me attack senior citizens and families. However, that does not wash. Clearly the Canadian public knows it does not wash. Two separate polls, one done in the fall of 1984 and another one published this January, show that around 22 per cent of the Canadian public feel that the deficit is the most important economic problem facing the country. Yet 54 per cent said unemployment was the major problem. Canadians felt that the deficit was a problem, but the majority did not consider increasing taxes or cutting back on social services was a viable means of reducing the deficit. However, those are the two steps which this Government has taken based on the philosophy of: The deficit made me do it.
The impact this Bill has is very broad. In one way or another it hits out at almost every sector of our economy. In committee we heard that this Bill would create more unemployment. Jobs in the steel and construction industries, the prestressed concrete industry, pet food and confectionery manufacturers would be lost right across the country. As well, it is unfair because a sales tax is regressive. It does not discriminate between those who can afford and those who cannot. Because of that, and because of the dollar value of the measures proposed through this Bill, it will hit lower income people to a much greater extent than those of us who have money left over.
Let me give you some examples. In 1986 a family with an average income of less than SI0,000 will pay about $128 more in taxes. For a family with an income between $30,000 and $35,000 the increase will be $352. For those making $50,000 or more the increase will be $547. However, when you look at the increase as a percentage of income, you find the numbers change and there is a greater impact on those with lesser
incomes. This Bill will take 1.39 per cent of the income of the family making less than $10,000; .92 per cent of those earning between $30,000 and $35,000; and only .69 per cent for those making over $50,000. Clearly this Bill takes money from people who can least afford it.
The National Council on Welfare, in its analysis of the Budget, found that poverty has been increasing dramatically. In 1981 there were approximately 3.5 million Canadians living in poverty. However, by 1984 that number had increased to 4.4 million, or 25 per cent. If we look at the average family income of the poorest fifth of Canadian families we see there has been a reduction of approximately 11 per cent. By comparison, the richest fifth of Canadian families realized a marginal increase of .6 per cent.
As I said at the beginning, this Bill is fairly wide reaching. It is part of the over-all package which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) introduced and it will take as much as $1,000 out of the pockets of a family of four earning $35,000 a year. Let me give you these figures because they show how this Government is approaching people in this country. The list includes the elimination of federal tax reduction, $100; modification to cost of living indexing, $115; cut in the family allowance, $22.50; broadening of the sales tax, $150; gas tax increase, $50; increase in oil and gas prices, $200; increase in sales tax, $150; increase in unemployment insurance premiums, $102; and cigarette and alcohol tax increase, $75; for a total family tax increase of $964.50. I have not included the cost of having to pay for a new social insurance card if you lose yours, airport parking, rail fares, or ferry service. The list goes on and on, Mr. Speaker.
Let us look at how Bill C-80 will impact on some of the sectors. Our municipalities are, by and large, supported by the property tax payers. This is another regressive tax because it does not take into consideration the ability of people to pay, nor does it take into consideration someone who has owned their own home for 40 or 50 years and has paid for it. It is not due to anything they did that the price went up and, therefore, the market value assessment went up. They do not see why their property taxes are at a certain level. They will be given an extra burden.
The Federation of Municipalities in Canada feels that this Bill will cost municipalities collectively $200 million every year. This comes at a time when the municipalities have done some very exhaustive research into their situation and find that we need a national program worth $12 billion just to protect the existing infrastructure of roads, bridges and sewers. Instead of working to help out the municipalities, the Government is giving them an extra $200 million bill each year. That bill will trickle down to the property tax payer. When Budgets are struck this spring in municipalities across the country, that will have to be considered. It may not show up as a line item or in zero-based budgeting, but it will certainly show up in the tax bill.

Farmers in Canada who are in a position to begin to expand their operations, perhaps by building a new silo, are going to find that the cost of a silo will be up by about $4,000. Our national trucking fleets move most of our food products in the country. As a result of the change in the gas tax, which is really a distance-related tax, truckers will have to pass more and more costs through to the consumer.
Let us take a look at the 1 cent per litre tax on gasoline which will come into effect on January 1, 1987, plus the 2 cent tax per litre which came into effect September 3, 1985. What will that do? We have heard in the Flouse over the last two weeks that world oil prices are falling extremely fast. Are Canadian gas prices falling as fast? Of course not. An industry that can respond immediately when world oil prices go up seems extremely sluggish when they go down.
My colleagues, the Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) and the Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) and I did a study in northwestern Ontario. We compared gasoline prices in northwestern Ontario with those of our neighbours to the south in Minnesota. On our side of the border a litre of gas costs anywhere from 53 cents in one of our more urban communities, to $1.80 per litre in some of the remote northern reserves. I remember the days when a gallon of gas cost much less than $1.80 in Thunder Bay. Now a litre costs $1.80 in some of those communities. A litre of gas in Minnesota, converted to Canadian funds, costs 38.4 cents to 44 cents. Clearly, Mr. Speaker, the American Government is more responsive to the change in world oil prices to ensure that its consumers get a break. In comparison, our Government is putting more taxes on.
It could be said that in some of our metropolitan communities, such as Toronto and Montreal, where there is an appropriate mix of urban transit, it perhaps makes sense to financially convince people to avail themselves of public transit. However, we do not have those options in northwestern Ontario. People who live in Atikokan do not have the option of using public transit. They no longer have rail service. If they need to get to Thunder Bay for medical assistance, for shopping, or for business, they have no choice but to drive the 120 miles each way. Northern residents all across the country are being penalized by this taxation.
I want to discuss for a moment the impact on the construction industry of the Budget and this particular Bill. The first issue I would like to discuss is the imposition of a new tax on the asphalt industry. Whether through the federal Government in terms of airport construction, through the provincial Governments in terms of highways, or through municipal Governments in terms of roads, governments are the main purchasers of those services. Bids are not put in one month with construction starting the next. In some cases it takes as long as three years from the

time a provincial government calls a tender until the asphalt is actually laid. Due to the provision of only a few months notice of the imposition of this tax, road construction firms across the country were forced to reduce, by the amount of the tax, the small profits they were making. subsubtopic: TRAGIC RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR HINTON, ALTA.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great sadness and sympathy that I rise today to report to the House on the collision between a freight train and a passenger railway train last Saturday, which tragically resulted in the loss of many lives. On behalf of the Government, and I am sure on behalf of all Members of the House and the people of Canada, I wish to extend my deepest sympathies and sincere condolences to the families of the victims of the collision. We share with them a tremendous sense of shock and grief at their loss. To those who suffered injuries, we extend our hopes and wishes for their early and complete recovery.
Over the weekend I spoke with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who has expressed his deepest personal sympathies and sorrow at this tragic event. Like all Canadians, he was horrified at learning of this tragedy. I have also been in contact with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), the Deputy Premier of Alberta, Mr. David Russell, and the Alberta Solicitor General, Ian Reid, who also extend their condolences and heartfelt thoughts to those involved.
At 8.45 a.m. on Saturday, February 8, VIA Rail train No. 4 travelling eastbound from Jasper and CNR freight train No. 413 travelling west from Edmonton collided at mile 173 of CN's Edson subdivision near Hinton, Alberta.
There were three crew members on the freight train, two at the front end and a conductor at the rear. On the basis of information currently available, the VIA passenger train carried a crew of 15, and 104 passengers had booked seats on the train. While search of the crash site and identification of bodies are still ongoing, it would appear that at least 29 people died as a result of the crash. The bodies have been taken to
Railway Disaster
Hinton where a temporary morgue has been established. The injured were rushed to hospitals in Hinton and Edmonton. Uninjured survivors were also taken to Edmonton and were assisted to complete their journey.
The track in the vicinity of the crash site is among the finest in North America. At this point it does not appear to have been a contributing factor. Likewise, the weather on Saturday morning was clear and cold and does not appear to be a likely contributing factor. While the CN train was carrying a limited amount of dangerous commodities, these were not involved in the collision or the resulting fire.
The first notification of the crash was received by CN within minutes. This information was immediately relayed to Hinton emergency services and the CTC, and the emergency response begun. Fire, police and paramedical units from Hinton arrived at the crash site and began the immediate task of rescuing survivors. Their efforts were hampered by fire at the site caused by the locomotive diesel fuel, and lack of ground access. Emergency response units from Hinton and CN assisted with the removal of the injured to surrounding hospitals.
On Sunday afternoon I visited the collision site and was horrified by the destruction that had occurred. I was moved and impressed by the dedication and the expertise with which rescue operations were conducted. I wish to commend the emergency response forces, and particularly those volunteers for their tireless efforts to rescue and comfort those involved in the collision. In particular I extend my appreciation to the residents of Hinton and the people of Alberta for the humanity and generosity that they have shared with the victims and their families.
I would also like to extend our appreciation to the office of the Hon. Member for Yellowhead, in particular Mr. David Jones at Edson whose efforts were invaluable in assisting the families and friends of the victims and those injured or surviving. As well, the co-operation and assistance of the Government of Alberta and provincial officials was greatly appreciated.
The safety of our transportation system is of paramount importance to this Government. We are deeply concerned by this tragedy, and believe that every effort must be made to determine the cause at the earliest possible date. Therefore, given the tragic and extraordinary circumstances surrounding this collision, the Government has ordered a judicial inquiry to ensure that a complete and independent examination takes place. I can inform the House that Justice Rene Paul Foisy of the Court of the Queen's Bench in Alberta has been appointed under Part I of the Inquiries Act to conduct the investigation. Mr. Justice Foisy has been given broad terms of reference to enable a comprehensive examination of the causes of this collision. We have also requested that the inquiry provide specific recommendations to reduce the risk of a reoccurrence of this tragic event. Mr. Justice Foisy has been asked to report

February 10, 1986
Railway Disaster
before May 30 so that the Government can have the benefit of his findings at the earliest possible opportunity.
In conducting the inquiry Mr. Justice Foisy will be able to draw on the work of the CTC accident investigators and staff who are presently conducting an extensive examination at the collision site. The CTC have five staff on site at present and another one is enroute. I have spoken to the CTC and they have assured me of their full co-operation with the inquiry. The latest information provided to me by the CTC suggests that there is evidence that the CN freight train ran through the switch joining the double-track to the single-track where the collision occurred. The switch was set for the passenger train, and the freight should have stopped on the double-track.
In conclusion, I wish to repeat again on behalf of the Prime Minister, our Government, and I trust all Members of the House, our heartfelt expressions of sympathy and compassion to the victims and families of those involved in this terrible railroad tragedy. We offer them our condolences, our sympathy and our prayers. Our Government is committed to an urgent and comprehensive inquiry into the causes and contributing factors relating to this collision. We have asked that interim measures be examined by the CTC to provide the necessary safeguards while the investigation is underway. The safety of the transportation system is a top priority and we are prepared to act on an urgent basis to respond to any safety deficiencies that can be identified.
The Canadian transportation system has a safety record amongst the best in the world. We must do all that we can to maintain and improve that record. As the Minister of Transport I commend to this House the Government's commitment to ensure that the safety of our transportation system is never diminished. We will use the full extent of our abilities and powers to safeguard the lives of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Liberal Party and my colleagues, I would like to add to the comments made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazan-kowski) by expressing our regret and sorrow to the families and relatives of the victims of the tragic train crash which occurred near Hinton, Alberta. I would like also to commend the emergency response forces which are on the site for, as the Minister has said, their tireless efforts to rescue and comfort those who were involved in this collision and, indeed, the residents of Hinton must be thanked for their efforts on behalf of the victims at the moment of the accident.
1 think we should recall at this time the words of Mr. Justice Samuel Grange in his report on the Mississauga train derailment. He said the following:
A long, fast train is a profitable one; it is not necessarily a safe one. I accept, of course, that in the course of natural justice one does not normally make an order affecting another's rights or pocket book without giving that other a chance to be heard. But there may come a time, where the safety of the citizen is concerned, when the onus shifts. In such case the burden of proof may (perhaps should) fall upon him who creates the risk.
I am sure all Members of the House would support the Minister of Transport if he were to put before us an immediate
program of measures designed to ensure that this type of accident is not repeated. Indeed, we have been very fortunate that in the past there have been very few fatalities, collisions and derailments. All rail companies have had, up to now, a solid safety record. However, this incident does raise a number of questions regarding the Government's record in and commitment to safety.
In transportation policy, the Government's sole crusade has been in the Fields of deregulation and cost recovery. We have as yet seen no positive commitment to safety. While we on this side of the House accept this new commission of inquiry and we will indeed assure the Government that we will co-operate with it on any measures that will enhance security for passengers using all modes of transportation, we must remind the Minister that this House has yet to see the implementation of the key safety recommendations contained in Judge Lockwood's Gimli inquiry, and in particular those contained in Barnard Deschenes' marine casualty investigation in which Recommendation No. 86 deals specifically with a multimodal safety board which would have powers similar to those of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board.
The Minister of Transport spent almost half a million dollars of taxpayers' money on Mr. Hugh Horner's Rail Passenger Action Force which did not even publish a final report. The result of that task force was the reintroduction of the Superliner in June 1986 on a very heavily travelled line. Since the public has yet to see this report, the Minister must now tell us what recommendations concerning safety were raised in this report that can no longer remain secret.
Finally, we know that the Treasury Board has instructed the Minister of Transport, under Structure 90, to cut back 600 person-years this fiscal year and 1,000 person-years next year. The Minister has failed to reassure us that this will in no way jeopardize his Department's responsibility in the field of safety. Indeed, we are waiting for more concrete, positive action on the part of the Government than merely another investigation.

subtopic: SIZE OF DEFICIT-CALL FOR THREE-PRONGED ATTACK BY GOVERNMENT
SIZE OF DEFICIT-CALL FOR THREE-PRONGED ATTACK BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the accumulated past debt symbolizes a kind of mismanagement which still shakes confidence in Canada. The debt is growing faster than our economy. Our debt, as a percentage of GNP, is one of the highest in the industrialized world. Recent downward pressure on the dollar and rising interest rates, while due in part to speculation, also reflect concern about the deficit and our resolve to do something about it.
Clearly, we must renew and strengthen our determination to deal with the deficit. The course charted in the November, 1984, economic statement and the May, 1985, Budget is correct. Most individual Canadians feel that they are now taxed to the limit. I think they are right.
I, therefore, suggest that the attack on the deficit should concentrate on three broad fronts; first, by reducing Government involvement and expenditure through the elimination of waste and the discarding of programs which are non-essential; second, by re-examining some social programs to direct payments only to those who are genuinely in need; and, third, by eliminating a number of corporate and individual preferences such as grants, exemptions, subsidies, investment tax credits, excessive capital cost allowances and tax deferrals. Deficit reduction will lead to renewed confidence, more growth, even more jobs, and greater prosperity for all Canadians.

Today and every day an ever-increasing number of Canadians ask the Prime Minister to restore Katimavik. Mr. Speaker,I wish to address this matter, inasmuch as I think the statement made by the Hon. Member is possibly a little general and sweeping with respect to the participation of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The Prime Minister did not at any point in time make any reference to statistics which were forthcoming from Statistics Canada. Indeed, that information, as I understand it, was in the hands of the media, specifically the CBC, which reported in advance of the actual day of announcement some details with respect to it.
With respect to the question of whether or not privileges have been affected one way or other, I do not think there is any basis or substance with respect to the Prime Minister having released any information at all.
Also, with respect to this matter, I understand that the Chief Statistician at Statistics Canada regards this as a serious matter which is important in terms of the operation of that agency. I also understand that he will be undertaking a serious examination of procedures in order to tighten them up.
As Your Honour will know, the current practice has been in effect for many years. That is to say, that there is a pre-release of this information to certain Departments, such as the Department of Finance, the Department of Employment and Immigration, the Office of the Privy Council, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and the Department of International Trade. The figures are released publicly within 24 hours of release to these officials, which has been the practice for many years.
As I indicated earlier, the fact that specific details were broadcast in advance by the media has caused the Chief Statistician to examine the circumstances to tighten up, hopefully, the procedures in order to ensure that this does not occur again.

I appreciate both arguments. I am sure that the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) takes this matter as seriously as does the agency. If the Hon. Member were bringing to me a case with respect to information which, perhaps, was included in an embargoed draft report of one of our parliamentary committees, or some such form, then there might be a question of privilege. However, given that the case he is raising is with regard to information which is properly the property of an agency of the Government and not of Parliament, it would be difficult for me to find that there is a case of parliamentary privilege, notwithstanding the quality of the Hon. Member's grievance and concern. Therefore, I find there is no prima facie case of privilege.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-80, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words regarding this legislation. It is legislation which will have enormous impact on ordinary Canadians. It implements key aspects of the May Budget. Specifically, it increases sales and excise taxes. A sales tax is simply a percentage tax on the price of goods we buy. It will have a direct and very important effect upon consumers. An excise tax is assessed at a fixed rate on units of things we purchase such as a litre of gasoline. This also will have a very dramatic effect upon the pocket-books of consumers across this country. Both taxes will hurt consumers. There is one positive but minor change in this legislation, and the Government deserves credit for it. The administration of the excise tax as it affects retailers is being changed so that when there is a dispute about the liability for tax, the collection of the tax can be delayed until the dispute is resolved. However, that does not take away from the over-all negative nature of the legislation.
This legislation will have enormous impact. Sales taxes are going to be increased on construction materials, cable and pay television services, alcoholic beverages, tobacco products and other goods. The total cost of the sales tax increases to Canadian consumers will be $990 million during the year 1986-87. Candy and confectioneries, soft drinks, pet foods, certain health foods and energy conservation equipment, all formerly exempt, are now subject to tax. it is a pretty mean Government that removes the tax exemption for candy bought by children with their allowance. The Government has chosen to take pennies out of the pockets of children in order to pursue this deficit fixation.

February 10, 1986
Excise Tax Act
Increasing taxes on health goods will also have a very real impact on elderly Canadians. It is not enough that the Government attempted to deindex old age pensions partially; it is now introducing sales taxes on the goods they need for health purposes. As well, energy conservation equipment is losing its exemption. With the world price of crude oil dropping, perhaps the Government has forgotten that energy conservation is crucial to the long-term economic health of this country. By doing this the Government is saying that it is not concerned at all with energy conservation. That is a very short-sighted and foolish policy for any Government. The fact that oil prices are dropping today does not mean they will continue to drop. In fact, we know the opposite will be the case.
The excise tax on gasoline and diesel and aviation fuel is going to be increased as well. When Members of the Government were in opposition they talked about world oil prices and a better deal for the consumer. Yet today we have falling world oil prices and prices at the pumps are being kept high by the companies who dominate the market. This Government has refused to take any effective action to bring those prices down. It has refused to use Petro-Canada as a lever in ensuring fair prices at the pump. Instead, the Government continues to maintain artificially high prices for gasoline. On top of that, it raises the taxes on gasoline.
Taxes on alcohol and cigarettes are also going up. There are obviously morale and health questions concerning the use of alcohol and cigarettes, many of which I am in sympathy with. Howerver, when the Government increases taxes on cigarettes and alcohol it simply takes another swipe at the consumer.
The total price tag for these increases to the consumer is something like $3.5 billion. That number is pretty hard to conceptualize, but it is an enormous amount. It is a tremendous burden on consumers at a time when they are feeling the pinch with regard to the cost of living. This measure shows the foolhardiness of the Government and its lack of concern for Canadians.
I could say many more things about these measures, but I will conclude my remarks. These measures are unfair in that they hit poor people more than they do wealthy Canadians. The Government could have found other sources of revenue. The negative economic impact of these measures has been documented as they affect most areas of the economy, particularly the tourism industry. Most of all, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that these tax measures affect low income Canadians more than they do upper income Canadians at a time when poverty is on the increase in the country. The Government should take note of the fact that the number of poor people in the country is increasing. Its tax policy should reflect that and it should show some concern for the people at the bottom end of the ladder.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I was glad to see that some Members on the government side are prepared to agree to this particular amendment. Members will know-
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, we agreed to the motion being put in the absence of the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap). We did not agree to the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I did not know whether the vote would be taken, whether in fact Members would be prepared to listen to the reasons for which my colleague, the Hon. Member for Spadina, who is our immigration critic, had hoped that the House would accept this particular amendment.
Members will know that the purpose of Bill C-55 is to allow the expansion of the Immigration Appeal Board from its present maximum of 18 members to a maximum of 50. They will also know that the Bill was put forward at the same time that the Plaut Report was being prepared looking at the question of refugee determination, and winding up proposals for alternative means of refugee determination
Members will know that the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration considered the Plaut Report and came back and endorsed most of its recommendations quite conclusively. The major one was that the Immigration Appeal Board should not be used as a chosen vehicle for making refugee determination decisions, but that there should be a separate board to do that difficult and very important job. The feeling that the committee had, the Plaut Commission had and certainly our Party has, is that the question of refugee determination is something that Canadians feel is important. We do not feel that people who are refugees should be forced out of Canada and sent back to homelands where they may risk death, imprisonment or persecution.
Now, how does this affect the amendment which is to limit the proposed increase in the size of the board to a maximum of 36 rather than the proposed 50? It affects it in this way: we have two processes going on side by side. On the one hand the Immigration Appeal Board is to be expanded, according to this Bill, to 50 members at a maximum. Yet on the other hand an all-Party committee has unanimously endorsed recommendations that refugee determination questions should be taken out of the hands of the Immigration Appeal Board. We know that originally the Government's proposal was that the board should be expanded to 36 members in order to deal with sponsorship and a number of other procedural questions where delays were beginning to take hold. I would assume that was done with the concurrence and agreement of the Government.
In future, if someone who claims refugee status on appeal and wishes to have an oral hearing before one member of the board, he or she may do so, but if he or she does not consent,
then the original procedure of a three-person appeal board and hearing will have to be followed. As I understand it, that means that the amendments to the appeal board portion of Bill C-55 will help to solve problems of work overload which the appeal board has been experiencing in a number of the other sections for which it is responsible. The board will not in the main resolve the question of refugee determination and, according to the recommendations of the Commons Standing Committee and of the Plaut Report, it should not do so. The Government will remain charged with the responsibility of acting on the Plaut Report, and l hope that means creating a convention refugee determination commission or board which will work on a non-adversarial basis, will not have to work only on the basis of the judicial rules of evidence, and will be able to make compassionate recommendations to the Ministry even in cases where it does not find that a prima facie case for refugee status actually exists. Those are matters on which the Government will have to make a decision.
The reason the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) and I are proposing that the size of the Immigration Appeal Board be restricted to a maximum of 36 members is, as we have argued before, that we do not want to see an appeal board, the existence of which has been questioned as recently as today in a long article in The Globe and Mail because of its failure or perceived failure to act in a quasi-judicial way due to problems in administration, perpetuated because of its vast size and become an institution. If this happens, the Government, because of its size, may be hesitant to cut back on, reorganize, or quite possibly, even eliminate or restructure it entirely. That is a fairly lengthy argument but that is why we are proposing that the maximum size be limited to 36 members rather than 50 as was originally proposed.
The compromise that refugee cases cannot be considered by a single-person panel except where the refugee claimant consents means that this is not now a Bill which is designed to eliminate the backlog of refugee applicants before the appeal board. Another procedure will have to be found. Under those circumstances, it does not make sense to go forward with an increase of the appeal board to 50 members when the reason for the increase to 50 members was that the Government thought at one time that it could use this particular device to eliminate the backlog.
I would like to conclude by saying that it is the opinion of my Party, and we think of most Canadians, that questions of refugee determinations which are life-and-death determinations in many cases must be dealt with in a very serious, thoughtful and sensitive way. A new procedure has been proposed by the Commons committee and by the Plaut Report. We hope that that procedure is followed and that the Government does not try to find some back-door way of doing indirectly what the committee determined in its hearings on Bill C-55 it should not be able to do directly. I do hope that the Hon. Minister of State will be able to consent to this particular amendment, which I think makes sense at this time, bearing in mind that the question of refugee determination is bound to come before the House again in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) who has been speaking on behalf of his Party's critic, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap). The Bill as it now stands, allows a far greater flexibility in terms of the role to be played by the IAB during this transition period.
