Mr. Speaker, as a member of the legislative committee and the standing committee, I urge Hon. Members to defeat Motion No. 1 on the basis of the following logic and information. As a result of the information which came to the committee from witnesses, it is not difficult to envisage that an expanded board of 50 members would take between two and three years to deal with the backlog of cases, not including refugee cases. It would deal simply with the backlog in terms of family reunification cases and the addition of rights of landed immigrants, which is contained in the Bill, to appeal to the Immigration Appeal Board on behalf of family sponsorship. With respect to the backlog and the increased workload with respect to family reunification cases, an expanded board of 50 members would take between two and three years to get caught up.
In its wisdom the committee amended the Bill before reporting it back to the House to ensure that these additional people will be employed by the Government of Canada to undertake that job on behalf of the people of Canada for a maximum term of two years. We are not instituting something by which people would be in place for five, 10 or 15 years. If Hon. Members would read carefully the amended Bill as reported from committee, they would see that appointees would be appointed for two-year terms only. One assurance we had from
the chairman of the board was that refugee claimants would not have their appeals heard by the board unless they requested it. In other words, any refugee claimant in the system has the power, through the system, to delay his hearing until a new system is put in place. The standing committee certainly dealt with the Plaut Report and with the refugee backlog. It has provided the Government with advice on how to deal with the matter.
However, I think the debate will advance more quickly and in better form if we do not cloud matters with the refugee issue. These commissioners are needed on the appeal board to deal with family reunification appeals. The increased number is not needed and will not be used in any major way to deal with the refugee cases. It is necessary to move as quickly as we can with respect to this issue. The suffering which is felt by a Canadian or a landed immigrant who wants to bring his or her mother, father, brother or sister to the country and is blocked at the appeal stage simply because of a lack of resources to hear the appeal is certainly a real tragedy.
I urge Hon. Members to limit the debate and to move as quickly as we can. If it is felt necessary, then a vote can be taken, if that is what members of the Opposition want. However, the faster we can recruit these new commissioners, train them and get them hearing cases, the more humanely will the Parliament of Canada be acting for some people who really need this type of help. The matter has been on our plate since June, and the faster we can deal with it the sooner more people in the country will be satisfied by the process.

Mr. Speaker, on January 27, I asked a question of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) concerning the future of the Prairie Wildlife Interpretation Centre near Webb, Saskatchewan. 1 would like now to expand on that subject because I perceive that no firm arrangements have been made for the 1986 summer season, and time is of the essence. The Centre is located some 17 miles west of Swift Current on the Trans-Canada Highway. It was opened in 1979. The visitors' centre and the adjoining lands cost in excess of $1 million. Paving of an access road in 1984 cost another $134,000.
The purpose of the centre was to display and interpret to visitors the unique wildlife to be found on the prairies. The centre was part of a network of five centres operated by the Canadian Wildlife Service which were marked in November, 1984 for transfer to the provinces or to the private sector. The other centres are in British Columbia, Ontario and two in the Province of Quebec. The operating budget of the Prairie Wildlife Centre for the 1983 season was $246,000. For 1984 it
was $217,000. In each of those years, approximately 20,000 visitors attended for a per person visit cost of between $11 and $12. Clearly, the centre was not being operated in an effective and efficient manner. It was, therefore, not unreasonable that some spending restraints be imposed.
I understand that some arrangements have been made for the continuing operation of the other four centres on a permanent basis. The problem with the Prairie Wildlife Centre relates directly to its location. It is representative of a vast semi-arid area of western Canada which, by its very nature, is sparsely populated. Southwestern Saskatchewan does not now, and likely never will have, a population base sufficient to support the centre to a break-even point.
The prairies ecology and wildlife is not well understood in Canada. This Centre is, therefore, important in its role of interpreting and translating the vibrancy and uniqueness of this region to visitors and locals alike. Closing the centre after the capital investment has been made and visitor patterns have been established is clearly unacceptable. Most people agree with the objective of cost reduction, but not to the extent of outright closure.
For the 1985 season, the operation was let to a private contractor and funded by the federal and Saskatchewan Governments to the sum of $68,000. This was to be an interim measure while negotiations continued toward the conclusion of a long-term contract. The 1985 summer season was somewhat less than satisfactory in that the opening was not announced until June 13, too late for adequate staffing, planning or preparation. Due to the late start last spring, a lack of marketing and the public perception that the centre was closed, attendance dropped to under 8,000. At the same time the net cost to the taxpayer, after deducting admission fees and land rentals, was under $50,000.
On October 16 last, I asked in this House as to the future of the centre. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Gurbin) stated in part that the Government intended to ensure that the centre remains open and serves the public. Again on January 27, in response to the same question,
I was most encouraged when the Minister replied in part: "The main thing is that we are going to keep that centre open and we are going to make an arrangement at an early date". It is now February 10 and I fear there will be a repeat of 1985. An immediate announcement is necessary. It will not be good enough to make an announcement in April, May or June. In order to give the centre a chance to prove itself sufficient, lead time is required.
Expo 86 opens on May 2 and there will be greatly increased traffic on the Trans-Canada Highway. This represents a tremendous opportunity to draw tourists to the centre, providing arrangements are in place. To gear up for May, the centre must have an operator and funding. There is much work to do and the hour is late. Staff must be hired, displays prepared and advertising done.
An area rancher has offered buffalo to the centre as an additional attraction. He deserves an answer. Each additional day of delay compounds the problem and leads to a less
February 10, 1986

satisfactory operation. We need an immediate announcement concerning 1986, the establishment of a telephone number, thus providing an opportunity for schools and other groups to book tours for May and June.
I urge the Minister to let a contract now for 1986 to the same operator as in 1985. That individual is familiar with the centre and is anxious to proceed. I further urge the Minister to redouble his efforts in seeking out a long-term solution to the future of the centre. The centre, in the short term at least, cannot survive on entrance fees and lease rentals. It is located in an area of sparse population but, nonetheless, an area with its own unique ecology and special wildlife heritage which is worthy of promotion and maintenance. That is the basis for its being and that remains the justification for its continuation.
The centre requires some Government support. I am not talking about vast sums of money. It is not a Cadillac type of operation. My constituents understand the enormity of the national debt and the paralysing effect that the interest charges which must be paid on that debt have. They appreciate that the operating budgets of the pre-1985 years are simply unacceptable relevant to that deficit. Clearly, the purpose of the centre, which is to display and interpret the unique wildlife of the prairie, is a worthy one. People in my constituency of Swift Current-Maple Creek want to see the centre continue. They also want to see it run effectively, efficiently, and at the least possible cost to the taxpayer.
I conclude by repeating that the successful operation of the Prairie Wildlife Interpretation Centre requires lead time for staffing, display preparation, program planning and advertising. Time is short. I respectfully urge an early and meaningful response in order that the centre can be opened in time to serve school groups, tourists and other members of the public.

subtopic: SENIOR CITIZENS-HOUSING NEEDS IN OWN NEIGHBOURHOODS
SENIOR CITIZENS-HOUSING NEEDS IN OWN NEIGHBOURHOODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 1, 1985, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) if the Government would consider a
Adjournment Debate
new policy directives with regard to the care of seniors in Canada. We have a tremendous need to preparing Canada and Canadians for the 21st century. Presently there are 2.6 million Canadian seniors, which is 10 per cent of the population. By the year 2021 there will be an estimated 5.9 million Canadian seniors, which will be 20 per cent of the population. That becomes a pressing problem. When the National Council on Aging filed its report in January of this year, it said that the number one concern of seniors, was shelter. Their concern is where they are going to live, in what neighbourhoods will they well spend their twilight years. When that concern is coupled with the fact that over 1 million Canadians today, mainly the young and young marrieds, are having problems finding housing, we can see a tremendous difficulty ahead in deciding how we are going to direct our resources and what our policies will be. Basically we have the question, how Canadians take care of their kin?
A couple of things have to happen in the area of housing. We have to look at what we have already done in our veteran's program through the initiative called the Aging Veterans Program with its home adaptation service and the home care service. The program has just recently been expanded from 8,000 to 18,000 veterans. It provides adaptations such as grab bars, locking systems on doors and, security systems, et cetera in veterans' homes. The cost of keeping them in their own homes is one-tenth that of putting veterans in a housing care facility for seniors. What a tremendous advantage this is. If we could expand this service to other seniors, not only would we save money, but seniors would be able to stay where they want to be, namely in their own homes.
We have portable flexible modular housing, which is added to an existing residence, this enables seniors could live with their families. These additions, also referred to as granny flats, are designed specifically for. I understand that Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation through its Design Committee is accepting proposals for new designs for the exterior and interior of housing for seniors. This report is due, I understand, in April.
These kinds of initiatives through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation will be of great help. At the same time, we have to find a way to bring home care to seniors in a wider context. We should investigate through our two ministries, of National Health and Welfare and Housing and Labour to see whether seniors can get vouchers for home care to pay for daily assistance to meet the needs and the responsibilities of running a house and living a normal life. Again are tremendous possibilities in this Field.
I realize the limitations because of federal and provincial responsibilities. A lot of health care is handed over to the provinces. Through some initiatives in these two ministries, the federal Government could show the lead and people would benefit.

February 10, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Canada is facing a major problem with an aging society which is starting to dominate in percentages. We are creeping up toward 20 per cent of the population in the over 65 age group. They are very healthy people because of diet and strides in medicine in the 20th century. They want to live in their own neighborhoods where they are comfortable with their friends to enjoy these years. We must find ways of keeping seniors in their homes with dignity. An extension of such programs as the Aging Veterans Program and extensions of CMHC's housing is important. We need to design housing that will not become a dinosaur. We have to get the dynamics of architecture involved so that we do not build something that is not needed in the 21st century.
We have over-built certain kinds of housing which no one else can use. In the latter part of the 20th century we overbuilt schools. The children who went to these schools are now forming the nucleus of what will be the graying society in the early part of the 21st century in Canada.
With some of these initiatives, Mr. Speaker, we could go on to bigger things.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Price (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: SENIOR CITIZENS-HOUSING NEEDS IN OWN NEIGHBOURHOODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for his representations on behalf of senior citizens. He is to be commended for his thoughtfulness and ingenuity in suggesting some solutions to a very serious problem.
When the Member first posed the question, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) replied that the Government is in complete agreement with the importance of helping seniors to live independently for as long as possible. It is without any hesitation that I repeat that position today.
That being said, I would like to inform the Member of the many initiatives through several Departments and agencies at the federal level that are already under way and that have the objective of helping our seniors to remain in their own homes for as long as possible.
Within the Department of National Health and Welfare, we are developing a strategy to promote health among older Canadians and to improve their quality of life. In the area of health services, we have produced guidelines for the establishment of services, such as day care centres since such centres have proved to be effective in postponing entry of the elderly into institutions. Other guidelines on rehabilitation services and on the prevention of progressive incapacity with aging are currently being prepared. In addition, the Department supports many projects to promote community living through its funding programs.
The Department is also actively exploring ways to promote independent living from a social service perspective. We are working very closely with homemakers associations across the country to improve training standards and to produce guidelines for the provision of adequate home care services. We also recognize that the income of seniors can influence their capacity to live independently. This is why we enhanced the financial situation of many of our seniors by expanding the Spouse's Allowance Program to all low income widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64. This goal has also led
us to discussions with the provinces aimed at improving the Canada Pension Plan.
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation also has this objective of independent living in mind in providing as many options as possible with respect to meeting the housing needs of seniors. These include funding research, as the Member has indicated, on innovative concepts such as granny flats and home sharing. It also means administering programs to help finance renovations and retrofitting of housing to make it more accessible and suitable. These programs are used heavily by seniors. Furthermore, CMHC has various social housing programs that add to the stock of housing for the elderly appropriate to independent living.
As indicated by the Hon. Member for London-Middlesex (Mr. Clifford), there are many Government departments involved in assisting seniors to live independently. Some I have mentioned, others the Member has mentioned. Veterans Affairs is another example. Although there is no single policy aimed at ensuring that seniors can remain in their own residences and thus improve their quality of life, there are many responses by the Government to that end.

subtopic: VISIBLE MINORITIES-REDRESS FOR JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II. (B) REQUEST THAT ACTION BE POSTPONED PENDING RECEIPT OF REPORT
VISIBLE MINORITIES-REDRESS FOR JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II. (B) REQUEST THAT ACTION BE POSTPONED PENDING RECEIPT OF REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate to review a question I asked in Question Period on January 28 of the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek). I referred to the ongoing dilemma of the Japanese Canadian redress.
The gist of my question on January 28 was two-fold. First, would the Minister show decency and patience to wait for a study and report commissioned by the Japanese Canadian community to look into the historical perspective of the losses and sufferings caused some 40 years ago. Second, was the Minister prepared to keep the commitment of his own Government to initiate a compensation package with the representatives of the National Association of Japanese Canadians.
The question was prompted by the Minister's Rambo-like actions the day before the Japanese association was in Ottawa. The Minister had met with the association, as did my Leader and myself, but in the press conference he referred to the national association as "dragging their feet" and as "trying to get their act together". He imposed, through those quotes, the deadline that unless the national association moved quickly and came to the Government table, he would perhaps proceed unilaterally as his predecessor attempted.
The editorials in the newspapers across the country the day after certainly took the Minister to task. I should like to refer to a few of them. The article in The Toronto Star captioned "Time for PM to intervene" read as follows:
It's time the Prime Minister, a man with proven skills as a negotiator, put an end to Jelinek's bullying tactics. Mulroney should take over the issue himself, and deliver an honourable settlement. That would be an act of leadership.
February 10, 1986

The article which appeared in the Vancouver Sun was captioned "Where's the fire?" and read:
Multiculturalism Minister Otto Jelinek's impatience to settle the issue of compensation for Japanese Canadians for the mistreatment they suffered during the Second World War is insensitive if not insulting.
The article in The Citizen entitled "Jelinek acting like Rambo in compensation wrangle" read:
One wonders just what exactly, then, the situation is. When Brian Mulroney was running for office, he spoke often of both apology and redress, something the Japanese Canadians warmly welcomed.
An editorial entitled "Mr. Jelinek's haste" in The Globe and Mail read:
This is the man Prime Minister Mulroney has entrusted with redressing what Mr. Mulroney has rightly called "an historic injustice." Can he not find someone with sympathy for the job?
An article written by Walter Stewart in The Toronto Sun and entitled "Jelinek shows his chutzpa" read:
It is that wrong that Jelinek now says Canada is willing to right. But only at his price, and only in his time. If he gets away with it, the crime will be compounded.
The whole thrust of those articles was simply to try to bring home to the Government, and particularly to the Minister, that the issue deserved the respect and sensitivity which other issues we debate in Parliament and throughout the country obtain. The Minister must keep the commitment offered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and by his predecessor, that they would mainly do two things: first, that they would negotiate compensation for the Japanese Canadian community. They said that very clearly, not only in speeches across the country but in a press release dated December, 1984. They also said that they would negotiate with the national association, the representative body of that constituency.
The Minister has spent considerable time on the differences which may exist within the Japanese Canadian community

differences of opinion, differences in approach and differences in process. That happens every day on virtually every issue we discuss in the Chamber. There is no unanimity on anything. There is no complete agreement on a process or a solution. In the end we try to build a consensus. We try to speak with and through the national organizations speaking for their constituencies. Whether it is The Canadian Bankers Association of the National Farmers Association, in the end we have a responsibility to deal with the structures that are in place and were elected by the constituencies they represent. I cannot see why the Minister chooses to spend most of his energy downgrading this national association. What he should be doing is negotiating, discussing and working closely with the national association so that together we can strike an agreement which will do us proud. He is not doing that.
Another factor is that the Minister is forgetting that the injustices to these individuals were against Canadian citizens, by and large. Ninety per cent of those individuals who lost their land, who lost their fishing boats, who lost their property, who lost their life savings, were Canadian citizens of Japanese ancestry. That does not change the fact that the rights of Canadians were abused. Therefore we should not only threat it
Adjournment Debate
as a minority issue or as a multicultural issue. It is not only that. It is wider. It speaks to the fundamental rights which you, Mr. Speaker, and I as Canadians enjoy today. Those Canadian rights, some 40 years ago, were trampled upon.
Perhaps the Minister of State for Multiculturalism-and I am saying this objectively-is not the appropriate Minister to be dealing with this issue. It is an issue of basic Canadian human rights. Rather than treating it from a multicultural perspective, perhaps we should have the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) dealing with what is essentially an injustice against Canadian citizens.

speakeroldname: Mr. Geoff Scott (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: VISIBLE MINORITIES-REDRESS FOR JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II. (B) REQUEST THAT ACTION BE POSTPONED PENDING RECEIPT OF REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it strikes me that the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) and 1 dealt with the Japanese Canadian redress issue not too long ago during an adjournment debate. I think the Hon. Member would agree that the issue is of such importance that it bears repeating and putting on the record, once again, the superb efforts of the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek) up to this point.
The Government continues to place high importance upon finding a just and equitable form of redress for Japanese Canadians, and upon finding a meaningful way to restore honour and dignity to Canadian citizens who were deprived of their rights and freedoms during World War II.
The Government believes that the matter of redress must be shared by all Canadians and therefore intends that any action on its part be done through Parliament on behalf of all Canadians. That is why, in our efforts to arrive at a reasonable solution, the Minister of State for Multiculturalism has undertaken to consult with a wide cross-section of Canadians represented by a variety of organizations, including provincial Governments.
Among those organizations, the National Association of Japanese Canadians is recognized as one of the most important representing the interests of Japanese Canadians. In a meeting with the NAJC on Monday, January 27, 1986, we were in general agreement on a number of principles. The Government has indicated its willingness to move forward on such items as: first, a formal acknowledgement and an apology for the events of 1942-43; second, a granting of pardon for those convicted of war-time infractions; third, the reinstatement of citizenship to those whose status was revoked; and, fourth, amendments to the War Measures Act to safeguard against future occurrences of that nature against any ethnic group.
The National Association of Japanese Canadians has commissioned a study by Price Waterhouse to try to determine the value of property and personal belongings lost as a result of the relocation. They have expressed a desire to await the results of that study and to have a complete redress package concluded which would include both monetary and non-monetary considerations.
While the Government sympathizes with that position, we are also aware that there are those in the Japanese Canadian

February 10, 1986
Adjournment Debate
community, including the more elderly survivors, who would like to have the issue resolved and out of the public domain as quickly as possible. Whatever the timing, the Minister of State for Multiculturalism, who I believe is doing an excellent job, and the Government of Canada will honour our commitment
to finding a just and equitable resolution as soon as practicable.
